Rule: Forcing a group to accept unwanted members intrudes on its internal affairs, but the right of expressive association isn't absolute. An infringement is justified by (all required): (1) a compelling state interest, (2) unrelated to the suppression of ideas, (3) that can't be achieved through means significantly less restrictive of association. Minnesota's interest in eradicating sex discrimination in public accommodations qualified, and the Jaycees showed no serious burden on the male members' expressive association.

Facts: The Jaycees (founded 1920 as the Junior Chamber of Commerce) limited regular membership to men 18 to 35; members took courses in public speaking and personal finance and joined charity, sports, and public-health programs. When the Minneapolis and St. Paul chapters admitted women, the national group moved to revoke their charters. The Minnesota Supreme Court held the Jaycees a "place of public accommodation" under the state Human Rights Act, which bars sex discrimination. Held: applying the Act didn't violate the First Amendment.

- Public accommodations history: state laws predated the federal Civil Rights Act of 1875; after the Court struck that Act in the Civil Rights Cases (1883), more states adopted them, and they were the main protection for disadvantaged groups until Congress returned to the field in 1957. Minnesota added sex in 1973.

- O'Connor's concurrence (now the influential view): the Court should first ask whether the group is an expressive association at all. A group engaged predominantly in protected expression gets strong protection for both its message and its choice of members; a commercial association gets only rational-basis review of its membership (a shopkeeper has no right to deal only with one sex). The Jaycees, a chamber of commerce that practices solicitation and management, was mainly commercial.

- Why it matters now: the casebook (quoting the Free Speech Center) says Boy Scouts of America v. Dale reinvigorated expressive association and implicitly rejected Brennan's approach in favor of O'Connor's, so the threshold "no serious burden" finding is what kept Roberts good law.

outline.title: Hurley v. Irish-American Gay, Lesbian and Bisexual Group of Boston, 515 U.S. 557 (1995)
outline.part: Chapter 14: Rights to Associate, to Assemble, and to Petition the Government
outline.text:
case · ch. 14
Hurley v. Irish-American Gay, Lesbian and Bisexual Group of Boston (1995)

Unanimous. Described in the casebook commentary and Klein's slides.

Rule: A parade is expression, and a speaker's choice not to propound a particular point of view is presumed to be beyond the government's power to control. Massachusetts couldn't use its public accommodations law to make the private organizers of Boston's St. Patrick's Day parade include a group marching under a gay-pride banner.

outline.title: Boy Scouts of America v. Dale, 530 U.S. 640 (2000)
outline.part: Chapter 14: Rights to Associate, to Assemble, and to Petition the Government
outline.text:
case · ch. 14
Boy Scouts of America v. Dale (2000)

5-4, Rehnquist, C.J., joined by O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, and Thomas. Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg, and Breyer dissented.

Rule: Forced inclusion of an unwanted person violates expressive association if (all required): (1) the group engages in expressive association (it needn't be an advocacy group; transmitting a system of values counts); (2) the person's presence would significantly affect the group's ability to advocate its viewpoints, a question on which courts accept the group's own account of its message; and (3) the state's interest doesn't justify so severe an intrusion. New Jersey couldn't make the Boy Scouts readmit an assistant scoutmaster who was a gay rights activist.

Facts: James Dale, a former Eagle Scout and assistant scoutmaster, had his adult membership revoked when the Boy Scouts learned he was gay and a gay rights activist. The New Jersey Supreme Court held the state's public accommodations law required his readmission. Held: that application violated the Scouts' right of expressive association.

- Deference: the Scouts said homosexual conduct conflicts with being "morally straight" and "clean." The Court accepted that assertion without further inquiry and rejected the state court's finding that the policy contradicted the Scouts' own goals: courts may not reject a group's values as unwise, irrational, or internally inconsistent. A group needn't trumpet its views, and tolerating internal dissent doesn't forfeit protection.

- Hurley parallel: the parade wasn't about sexual orientation either, but the organizers could still exclude a contingent; likewise the Scouts may choose to send one message and not another.

- Public accommodations laws have expanded from inns, trains, restaurants, and hotels to membership groups like the Scouts, and to more protected classes (beyond those that get heightened equal protection scrutiny), so conflicts with association have grown. Roberts was distinguished because the Jaycees showed no serious burden.

- Stevens's dissent stressed changing public attitudes toward homosexuality; the majority answered that growing acceptance of an idea is all the more reason to protect those who disagree.

outline.title: Compelled Speech, Again
outline.part: Chapter 14: Rights to Associate, to Assemble, and to Petition the Government
outline.text: Rule: Outside the commercial-speech context, government almost never may compel private speech: it may not make a person speak its preferred message (West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette; Wooley; NIFLA) or force a speaker to include others' ideas in its own expression (Hurley). But a law that regulates conduct with only incidental effects on speech, or that gives outsiders access without making them members, doesn't compel speech or association (FAIR).

outline.title: Rumsfeld v. Forum for Academic and Institutional Rights, 547 U.S. 47 (2006)
outline.part: Chapter 14: Rights to Associate, to Assemble, and to Petition the Government
outline.text:
case · ch. 14
Rumsfeld v. Forum for Academic and Institutional Rights (2006)

Unanimous, Roberts, C.J. Alito, J., recused.

Rule: Because Congress could impose the Solomon Amendment's equal-access requirement directly, conditioning federal funds on it isn't an unconstitutional condition. The law regulates conduct, not speech: (1) any compelled speech (e.g., sending a scheduling e-mail for the military recruiter) is merely incidental to the conduct regulation; (2) hosting recruiters isn't inherently expressive like a parade, so it doesn't interfere with the schools' message, and nobody would think the schools endorse the recruiters; and (3) it doesn't burden association, because recruiters are outsiders on campus briefly, not members of the school.

Facts: Law schools that opposed "Don't Ask, Don't Tell" (which required discharging service members who said they were gay) barred military recruiters under their nondiscrimination policies. Congress responded with the Solomon Amendment: if any part of a university denied military recruiters access equal to other recruiters, the whole university lost certain federal funds. FAIR, an association of law schools and faculties, sued; the Third Circuit ordered a preliminary injunction. Held: reversed; no First Amendment violation.

- Schools remain free to speak: they may say whatever they like about the military's policy while keeping their funds, and students and faculty may associate to protest.

- Trivializing Barnette and Wooley: comparing a recruiting e-mail to a compelled pledge or a compelled "Live Free or Die" plate, the Court said, trivializes those freedoms.

- Contrast Dale: the Solomon Amendment doesn't force a school to accept members it doesn't want.

outline.title: 303 Creative LLC v. Elenis, 600 U.S. 570 (2023)
outline.part: Chapter 14: Rights to Associate, to Assemble, and to Petition the Government
outline.text:
case · ch. 14
303 Creative LLC v. Elenis (2023)

6-3, Gorsuch, J., joined by Roberts, C.J., Thomas, Alito, Kavanaugh, and Barrett. Sotomayor, J., dissented, joined by Kagan and Jackson.

Rule: A state may not apply its public accommodations law to compel a person to create speech she doesn't believe. Where the parties stipulated that custom wedding websites are original, expressive "pure speech," Colorado couldn't force Lorie Smith to design sites celebrating same-sex weddings. Being paid, and working through a company she alone owns, doesn't change that. Public accommodations laws remain valid across a vast array of ordinary goods and services; when one collides with the Constitution, the Constitution prevails.

Facts: Smith's business, 303 Creative, offers website and graphic design. She planned to add wedding websites telling each couple's story, with her company's name on every site. She will serve customers of any sexual orientation but won't create content that contradicts her religious belief that marriage is between one man and one woman, whoever orders it. Colorado's anti-discrimination law forbids businesses open to the public from discriminating by sexual orientation. Held: applying the law to compel her speech violates the Free Speech Clause.

- Lineage: Brandeis in Whitney (speech as an end and a means), Barnette's "fixed star," Wooley, NIFLA, Hurley, Dale, Snyder, Counterman, and the Skokie march: a commitment to speech for only some messages and some speakers is no commitment at all.

- Compelling interest acknowledged: states have a compelling interest in eliminating discrimination in public accommodations (Roberts v. U.S. Jaycees), and protecting gay persons is "unexceptional" (Masterpiece Cakeshop), but Hurley and Dale show such laws can't be applied to compel expression.

- Sotomayor's dissent: for the first time the Court gives a business open to the public a constitutional right to refuse service to a protected class. The law targets the conduct of discrimination, not speech, and discrimination has never been protected expression; she quoted Masterpiece Cakeshop's "general rule" that religious and philosophical objections don't let businesses deny protected persons equal access under neutral and generally applicable public accommodations laws.

- The casebook's questions: what exactly is the holding? Could a state make a baker sell an undecorated wedding cake to a same-sex couple, and how is that different from a custom website? (The opinion rests on the stipulation that every website is the designer's own expressive creation; selling an off-the-shelf product on equal terms is ordinary conduct.)

outline.title: Synthesis: Association and Compelled Speech
outline.part: Chapter 14: Rights to Associate, to Assemble, and to Petition the Government
outline.text:
Case | What the government did | Result | Key reason
NAACP v. Alabama (1958) | Demanded member names and addresses | Group wins (unanimous) | Disclosure would expose members to reprisal and chill association; no controlling justification
First Choice (2026) | Subpoenaed donor information | Group has standing (9-0) | Donor demands chill association even if kept confidential (AFP v. Bonta)
Roberts v. U.S. Jaycees (1984) | Required admitting women as members | State wins | Compelling interest in ending sex discrimination; no serious burden on expression
Hurley (1995) | Required a parade to include a gay-pride contingent | Organizers win (unanimous) | A parade is expression; a speaker may decline to propound a view
Boy Scouts of America v. Dale (2000) | Required readmitting a gay assistant scoutmaster | Group wins (5-4) | Expressive group; significant burden on its message, as the group describes it
Rumsfeld v. FAIR (2006) | Conditioned funds on equal access for military recruiters | Government wins (unanimous) | Regulates conduct; speech incidental; recruiters aren't members
303 Creative (2023) | Required a designer to make same-sex wedding websites | Designer wins (6-3) | Compels creation of pure speech; pay and corporate form irrelevant

- Pattern: compelled disclosure and compelled membership or message usually lose for the government under strict scrutiny; compelled access or ordinary conduct with incidental speech effects usually wins (FAIR; selling ordinary goods on equal terms).

- Threshold questions decide most cases: is the group expressive, or mainly commercial (O'Connor in Roberts)? Is the regulated activity speech or conduct?

outline.title: Stretch Exercise: The Wedding Photographer and Line-Drawing
outline.part: Chapter 14: Rights to Associate, to Assemble, and to Petition the Government
outline.text:
After 303 Creative, a district court ruled largely for a wedding photographer who challenged New York's public accommodations law, holding wedding photography expressive and that New York couldn't compel her to create content celebrating same-sex weddings. Does that follow directly from 303 Creative, and what is the counterargument?

- Where's the line? A stationer printing invitations (for same-sex or interracial couples), a hair stylist, a make-up artist, a florist, a caterer, a limo driver. Ask how much each creates an original, customized message the creator is identified with (photographer, designer, perhaps stationer) versus providing a service or product that is ordinary conduct (limo driver, caterer). Then ask how to weigh First Amendment values against the state's interest in preventing discrimination.

- Barnette's limit: Justice Jackson stressed that the Barnette children's freedom didn't collide with anyone else's rights; they only wanted to stand silently. In 303 Creative the speaker's right was set against customers' interest in equal service. Should that distinction matter?

- Test your principles by swapping facts: imagine a designer who refuses to create racist or homophobic content, or a stylist who refuses a customer wearing a shirt with racist slogans. Does your view of when businesses must serve everyone change?
